h:
Someone told you the Book of Enoch contradicts the Bible.

They quoted Jesus. Matthew 22:30.

“In the resurrection they neither marry nor are given in marriage, but are like angels in heaven.”

Angels don’t marry, they said. So Enoch is wrong. So Genesis isn’t about angels taking wives. So the Nephilim aren’t real hybrids.

Here’s the problem. Their own Bible demolishes this argument in three verses.

First: Read what Jesus actually said.

“Angels in heaven.”

Not angels everywhere. Not angels in all circumstances across all time. Angels in heaven, in their proper dwelling, in their unfallen state.

The Watchers weren’t in heaven. That’s the entire point.

Jude 6, three books after Matthew in your own New Testament:

“The angels who did not stay within their own position of authority, but left their proper dwelling, he has kept in eternal chains under gloomy darkness until the judgment of the great day.”

Left their proper dwelling. The Greek is oiketerion. Their own habitation. The place where angels in heaven don’t marry because that’s not what they do there.

The Watchers left. That’s not Enoch’s claim. That’s Jude’s claim. In the canon.

So when someone quotes Matthew 22:30 to dismiss the Watcher narrative, they’re using a verse about angels who stayed in heaven to argue against angels who left heaven.

The verse doesn’t apply. It describes a different category of being in a different location doing a different thing.

Second: Read what Peter said.

2 Peter 2:4. Still in your Bible.

“God did not spare angels when they sinned, but cast them into hell and committed them to chains of gloomy darkness to be kept until the judgment.”

Angels who sinned. Cast into hell. Chains. Judgment pending.

What sin?

Peter doesn’t specify here. But Jude does, in a parallel letter written to the same audience about the same events. The sin was leaving their proper dwelling to pursue strange flesh.

Two New Testament authors, writing independently, both referencing angels who sinned in a specific way, both describing the same punishment: chains, darkness, held for judgment.

Neither of them thought angels couldn’t sin. Neither of them thought the category of “angels doing things they weren’t supposed to do physically” was theologically impossible.

They wrote about it as established fact their readers already knew.

Because their readers had Enoch.

Third: Read Genesis and ask what it actually says.

“The sons of God saw that the daughters of man were attractive. And they took as their wives any they chose.” (Genesis 6:2)

“The Nephilim were on the earth in those days, and also afterward, when the sons of God came in to the daughters of man and they bore children to them.” (Genesis 6:4)

Sons of God. Hebrew: bene ha’elohim.

That phrase appears four other times in the Old Testament. Job 1:6. Job 2:1. Job 38:7. Daniel 3:25.

Every single time, without exception, it refers to heavenly beings presenting themselves before God. Not humans. Not Seth’s descendants. Not godly men from the right genealogy.

Heavenly beings.

The Sethite interpretation, the idea that “sons of God” just means Seth’s godly line marrying Cain’s ungodly line, was invented by Augustine in the 4th century.

Not discovered. Invented.

Because Augustine’s Platonic theology required angels to be non-physical. Because a physical angel capable of reproduction was too strange for Greek philosophical categories.

But the text doesn’t say Seth’s line. It says bene ha’elohim. And it says the offspring were the Nephilim, the gibborim, the mighty men of renown. Seth’s line marrying Cain’s line produces ordinary humans.

The text says they produced something that is described in the same terms ancient mythology uses for demigods and divine heroes. Because that’s what they were.

The historical witness they can’t explain away.

The earliest Jewish interpreters understood Genesis as angelic. The Book of Enoch, written before the New Testament, treats it as documented history. Jubilees treats it as documented history.

The Dead Sea Scrolls community treats it as documented history. Josephus, the Jewish historian, treats it as documented history.

The early church fathers understood it the same way.

Justin Martyr. Irenaeus. Clement of Alexandria. Tertullian. Origen. All of them read “sons of God” as angels. All of them knew the Watcher narrative. All of them treated Enoch as authoritative.

The shift came in the 3rd and 4th centuries. Cambridge scholar Annette Yoshiko Reed documents that church leaders rejected the angelic reading specifically by following the rabbis, the same rabbis who had rejected the Messiah, who changed bene ha’elohim to “sons of judges” to distance themselves from the Enochic framework.

The Western church followed the rabbis who rejected Jesus to arrive at an interpretation that dismisses the text that explains Jesus’s genealogy.

Read that again.

Meanwhile, Ethiopia preserved the full canon in the mountains.

The argument proves too much.

“Angels can’t marry” doesn’t just dismiss Enoch.

It dismisses Jude 6. It dismisses 2 Peter 2:4. It dismisses the plain reading of bene ha’elohim across five Old Testament texts. It dismisses the unanimous witness of the earliest Jewish and Christian interpreters.

It dismisses the question of why the Flood was necessary at all if the corruption was just ordinary human sin.

It dismisses your own Bible to protect an interpretation invented 400 years after the New Testament by a man whose theology was shaped more by Plato than by Moses.

Genesis says the sons of God took wives and produced giants.

Jude says angels left their proper dwelling and are chained for it.

Peter says angels sinned and are imprisoned pending judgment.

The argument that angels can’t do what three biblical authors say angels did isn’t biblical defense.

It’s damage control.
